titleStmt.title: Improved Schedulability Tests for Global Fixed-Priority Scheduling

analytic.title: Improved Schedulability Tests for Global Fixed-Priority Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In this paper, global fixed-priority multiprocessor scheduling of a set of sporadic real-time tasks is addressed. First, we propose a priority-assignment policy, called ISM-US, for implicit-deadline task systems. Policy ISM-US assigns slackmonotonic priorities to a subset of the given task set and other tasks are assigned the highest fixed priority. We prove that the schedulability utilization bound for policy ISM-US is higher than the corresponding bound for any other existing schedulability test for implicit-deadline sporadic task systems. Second, we propose improvements to two state-of-the-art iterative schedulability tests for constrained-deadline sporadic task systems. Our improved schedulability tests, called HP-RTA-LC and HP-DA-LC, are based on a hybrid-priority assignment policy and are shown to dominate the two existing state-of-the-art tests, RTA-LC and DA-LC, respectively.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Consider the following problem: Given a collection of n constrained-or implicit-deadline sporadic tasks, is it possible to meet all the task deadlines when the tasks are fixed-priority (FP) scheduled on m identical, unitcapacity processors? Real-time tasks scheduling on multiprocessors is primarily based on either global or partitioned approach. In global scheduling, a task is allowed to execute on any processor even when it is resumed after preemption. In partitioned scheduling, the task set is grouped in different task partitions during design time and each partition has a fixed processor on which only the tasks of that partition are allowed to execute. The main design goal of many global [2], [5], [8], [1], [9], [7], [15], [12] and partitioned [3], [14], [17] FP scheduling algorithms is to derive a schedulability test that when satisfied implies that all the deadlines are met.

One of the most popular and expressive ways to derive a schedulability test for a scheduling algorithm is in terms of its utilization bound. It has already been proved that neither global nor partitioned FP scheduling can have a utilization bound greater than 0.5m on m processors for implicit-deadline task systems [2], [17]. There exists a partitioned FP scheduling algorithm, called R-BOUND-MP-NFR, having utilization bound of 0.5m [3]. However, the best state-of-the-art utilization bound of global FP multiprocessor scheduling is m+1 3 for m ≤ 6 (RM-US[ 1 3 ] scheduling [8]) and 2m 3+ √ 5 for m > 6 (SM-US scheduling [1]) for implicitdeadline sporadic task systems. Our first contribution in this paper is proposing a new FP assignment policy, called Improved SM-US (ISM-US), for implicit-deadline sporadic task systems. We prove that the utilization bound of global FP scheduling using policy ISM-US is higher than that of both RM-US[ 1 3 ] and SM-US for implicit-deadline task systems for any finite m ≥ 2.

The iterative schedulability test is another approach to testing the schedulability of a task set for global FP scheduling. The basic idea of the iterative approach is that one condition is tested for each lower priority task. Several works have proposed iterative tests for global FP scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic task systems [8], [7], [9], [15], [11]. By combining the ideas from [7], [6], Guan et al. [15] proposed an iterative test for constrained-deadline task systems, here referred to as "RTA-LC", that calculates upper bounds on the response time for each sporadic task. Recently, inspired by that work, Davis et al. [12] proposed a new iterative test, called DA-LC, that is an improvement of the test proposed by Bertogna et al. [9] for constraineddeadline sporadic task systems. It has been shown in [12] that, for any given FP ordering of the tasks, the RTA-LC test dominates the tests in [7], [9] as well as the DA-LC test.

The work in [12] derives an effective joint priority assignment policy and schedulability test by combining the DA-LC test in [12] with Audsley's optimal priority assignment (OPA) algorithm [4]. It is empirically shown in [12] that the combination of OPA and DA-LC outperforms the RTA-LC test regardless of what heuristic priority assignment policy (e.g., deadline-monotonic) the latter uses. It is also proved in [12] that the combination of OPA and DA-LC is the optimal fixed-priority assignment policy when using the DA-LC test.

Regarding the optimality of the combination of OPA and DA-LC in [12], we observe that it is possible to further improve the performance of this approach. The reasons for this are that (i) optimality is only claimed under the assumption that the entire task set and all processors are involved when this combination is used for determining the fixed-priority ordering of all the tasks and (ii) the details of the schedulability analysis in [15], [12] imply that, if not all tasks and processors are included in the analysis, the interference of a higher priority task (calculated based on the RTA-LC or DA-LC test) on a lower priority task may be reduced. Based on this finding, our second contribution in this paper is proposing a new priority assignment policy for DA-LC that performs better than the combined use of OPA and DA-LC. Our new priority-assignment policy is based on a hybrid-priority assignment (HPA) policy: for some k < m, each task in a subset of k tasks of the entire sporadic task set is given the highest fixed priority and the remaining (nk) tasks are given other, lower, fixed priorities. While the OPA algorithm is not (as shown in [12]) applicable to RTA-LC, we find that our HPA policy is indeed applicable to RTA-LC.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents related work. Then, the task model is presented in Section III. The priority assignment policy ISM-US and its corresponding utilization bound for implicit-deadline task system is proposed in Section IV. We then present the improved priority-assignment policy for the state-of-the-art iterative tests for constrained-deadline task system in Section V. Experimental results to estimate this improvement are presented in Section VI. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section VII.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The HPA policy has been used in the development of numerous global FP scheduling algorithms and their corresponding schedulability tests, the first being the RM-US[ m 3m-2 ] algorithm proposed by Andersson, Baruah and Jonsson [2]. That algorithm was shown to have a utilization bound of m 2 3m-2 on m processors for implicitdeadline tasks. The RM-US[ m 3m-2 ] algorithm manages to avoid the so-called "Dhall's effect" [13] by assigning the highest fixed priority to the tasks having utilization greater than m 3m-2 while the rest of the tasks are assigned priorities according to the traditional Rate-Monotonic (RM) policy.

In [5], Baker presented an analysis of global FP scheduling. Based on a derivation of the minimum amount of interference in an interval that can cause a task's deadline to be missed, Baker showed that, for implicit-deadline sporadic task sets, the utilization bound of RM scheduling is m(1-umax) 2 + u min , where u max and u min are the maximum and minimum utilization of any task in the task set, respectively.

Bertogna et al. [8] proposed an improvement of the algorithm in [2], called RM-US[ 1 3 ] for implicit-deadline sporadic task systems. Based on schedulability analysis of the deadline-monotonic priority assignment, Bertogna et al. proved that the utilization bound of the a HPAbased RM-US[ 1 3 ] algorithm is m+1 3 for implicit-deadline tasks. Andersson [1] proposed an algorithm based on a slack-monotonic HPA policy that has a utilization bound of 2m 3+ √ 5 for implicit-deadline sporadic task systems. In that algorithm, called SM-US, each task having utilization greater than 2 3+ √ 5 is given the highest fixed priority while the rest of the tasks are assigned slack-monotonic priorities.

The current state-of-the-art utilization bound for global multiprocessor scheduling of implicit-deadline sporadic tasks is m+1 3 for m ≤ 6 (RM-US[ 1 3 ] scheduling [8]) and 2m 3+ √ 5 for m > 6 (SM-US scheduling [1]). In this paper, we propose a new slack-monotonic HPA policy, called ISM-US, and prove that its corresponding utilization bound for global FP scheduling of implicit-deadline sporadic tasks

}, which is higher than that of both RM-US[ 1 3 ] and SM-US for any finite m ≥ 2. Recently, based on Baker's analysis in [5], several works [9], [7], [15] have proposed iterative schedulability tests for constrained-deadline sporadic task systems. In [9], [7], [15], the work done by a job of a higher-priority task τ i is considered as "carry-in" work within the scheduling window of a lower-priority task τ k , if τ i has partially executed strictly prior to the beginning of the window. If a higher-priority task is considered to constitute carry-in work, then its worst-case interference on the lower-priority task is higher than that of its non-carry-in counterpart [15], [12].

The global FP schedulability analysis of a lower-priority task τ k in [9], [7] considers all the higher-priority tasks to have carry-in work. Baruah's global EDF schedulability analysis in [6] limits the number of higher-priority tasks considered to have carry-in work to (m -1). The RTA-LC test ("LC" stands for "Limited-Carry") proposed by Guan et al. [15] employs the same carry-in task-limitation as in [6] to improve the response time analysis in [7] for FP scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic tasks. Recently, inspired by the works in [7], [6], [15], the DA-LC test proposed by Davis et al. [12] also consider (m -1) tasks having carry-in work to improve the schedulability analysis in [9] for global FP scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic tasks.

The RTA-LC test dominates the DA-LC test for any given fixed-priority ordering of the constrained-deadline tasks [12]. However, Davis et al. [11], [12] addressed the problem of finding an effective priority assignment using Audsley's OPA algorithm [4] for the class of schedulability tests that are OPA-compatible 1 . To that end, RTA-LC is proved not to be OPA-compatible while DA-LC is proved to be OPA-compatible [12]. It is empirically shown that OPA combined with DA-LC is currently the best combination of priority-assignment policy and schedulability test for global FP scheduling [12].

In this paper, we use the HPA policy to improve the priority-assignment policy for the combination of OPA algorithm and DA-LC test (note that the HPA policy is not explored in [15], [12]). While the OPA algorithm cannot be applied to RTA-LC, we find that the HPA policy can be successfully applied to find an effective combination of priority-assignment policy and RTA-LC test.

div.head: III. TASK MODEL
div.p: In this paper, we consider global preemptive scheduling of n independent sporadic tasks in set Γ ={τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . τ n } on m identical, unit-capacity processors. Each task τ i ∈ Γ is characterized by a triple (C i , D i , T i ), where C i represents the worst-case execution time (WCET), D i is the relative deadline, and T i is the minimum inter-arrival time of the instances of task τ i . Successive arrivals of the instances (called jobs) of task τ i are separated by at least T i time units. Each job of task τ i requires at most C i units of execution time before its relative deadline. A task system Γ is called implicit-deadline task system if the relative deadline of each task is equal to its minimum inter-arrival time. A task system Γ is called constrained-deadline task system if the relative deadline of each task is less than or equal to its minimum inter-arrival time. For a given fixed priority ordering of the tasks, the set of tasks with a priority higher than τ k is denoted by hp(k).

div.head: IV. TEST FOR IMPLICIT-DEADLINE TASK SYSTEMS
div.p: Our proposed priority-assignment policy ISM-US for implicit-deadline sporadic task systems is based on a slackmonotonic HPA policy that works as follows: if the utilization of a task is not greater than a threshold utilization, say u ts , then the task is assigned a priority according to the slack-monotonic policy; otherwise, the task is given the highest fixed priority. In the slack-monotonic priorityassignment policy, the smaller the difference (slack) between a task's relative deadline and WCET, the higher is the assigned priority.

The threshold utilization u ts for policy ISM-US is determined based on the schedulability analysis of a class of task sets, called "special" task sets. A task set is said to be "special on m processors" based on two particular properties (defined shortly in Definition 1). We prove that the utilization bound of global FP scheduling of sporadic tasks using policy
div.formula: ISM-US is m•min{ 1 2 , 3m-2- √ 5m 2 -8m+4 2m-2

div.p: The proof strategy we follow to derive the utilization bound is as follows. First, we show that a "special" task set Γ k (which is a subset of the original task set Γ) is schedulable by global FP scheduling based on slack-monotonic priority assignment (subsection IV-B). Second, we derive two general conditions that imply that the entire task set Γ is schedulable using a slack-monotonic HPA policy that uses some threshold utilization u ts (subsection IV-C). Finally, we determine the value of the threshold utilization u ts for policy ISM-US and derive the corresponding utilization bound for global FP scheduling of the entire task set (subsection IV-D). The following definitions and results in subsection IV-A will be used in the remainder of this section.

div.head: A. Useful Definitions and Prior Results
div.p: Without any loss of generality, we assume that the tasks in Γ are sorted based on decreasing priority order. Whether task τ k meets its deadline or not depends only on the tasks in set hp(k) ∪ {τ k }. We find it useful to define the task set Γ k def = hp(k) ∪ {τ k } where τ k is the lowest priority task in Γ k and hp(k) = {τ 1 , . . . , τ k-1 }, for k = 1, 2 . . . n. Note that Γ j ⊆ Γ k for j ≤ k.

We define the utilization of a task τ i as u i = C i /T i and the total utilization of the task set Γ k as U k = τi∈Γ k u i for k = 1, 2 . . . n. We define the maximum utilization u k max and the minimum utilization u k min of a sporadic task system Γ k to be the largest and smallest utilization of any task in Γ k , respectively.

div.head: B. "Special" task set and its Schedulability
div.p: In this subsection, we formally define the two properties of a sporadic task system Γ k that is "special" on m processors and we prove that all the deadlines of the special task system Γ k are met using global slack-monotonic scheduling (i.e., global FP scheduling using slack-monotonic priority assignment), denoted by GS SM , on m processors. div.head: C. Slack-Monotonic Hybrid Priority Assignment
div.p: According to our (improved) slack-monotonic HPA policy ISM-US, the priorities to the tasks are assigned based on some threshold utilization u ts such that all the tasks having utilization not greater than u ts are given the slack-monotonic priorities and each task having utilization greater than u ts is given the highest fixed priority. Using such hybrid policy, the sporadic task set Γ is visualized as the union of two sets Γ = Γ L ∪ Γ H such that the tasks in set Γ L have the slackmonotonic priorities and each task in set Γ H has the highest fixed priority.

Before the threshold u ts for the priority assignment policy ISM-US is determined, we present two general conditions, denoted as C1 and C2, in Lemma 5 that can imply the feasibility of a task set based on HPA policy ISM-US. Lemma 5. Let u ts be the threshold utilization that is used to determine the sets Γ L and Γ H such that Γ = Γ L ∪ Γ H assuming the priority assignment policy ISM-US. The sporadic task set Γ is schedulable using global FP scheduling if the following two conditions C1 and C2 are satisfied

It is also implied in [2], [1] that the predictability of global FP scheduling has the following consequence: if the jobs of a task τ i are schedulable considering WCET equal to C ′ i such that C ′ i = T i using global FP scheduling A on m processors, then the jobs of τ i are also schedulable considering its WCET equal to C i using A on m processors.

Observation 1: HPA policy can guarantee the schedulability of an implicit/constrained-deadline task set using global FP scheduling if k highest utilization/density 2 tasks are given the highest fixed priority and the remaining (n-k) lowest utilization/density tasks are global FP schedulable on (mk) processors using some other fixed priority assignment, for some k, 0 ≤ k < m. Now, based on the two general conditions (C1 and C2) of Lemma 5, the threshold utilization u ts for priority assignment policy ISM-US and its corresponding utilization bound of global FP scheduling of an implicit-deadline sporadic task set Γ is presented in subsection IV-D.

div.head: Theorem 2. An implicit-deadline sporadic task set Γ is schedulable using global FP scheduling that assigns the priorities based on policy ISM-US

div.p: Proof: Given the task set Γ and the number of processors m, we can determine the two subsets Γ L and Γ H such that Γ = Γ L ∪ Γ H based on the threshold utilization u ts = B(m). We will show that if the total utilization U n ≤ m • min{1/2, B(m)}, then the two general conditions C1 and C2 of Lemma 5 hold; which guarantees the schedulability of Γ using global FP scheduling.

(C1 holds) It is easy to see that B(m) ≥ min{1/2, B(m)}. Then it follows that each task in Γ H has utilization greater than min{1/2, B(m)} since each task in Γ H has utilization greater than u ts = B(m) for HPA policy ISM-US. If the total utilization (i.e., U n ) of Γ is not greater than m • min{1/2, B(m)}, then the number of tasks that are given the highest priority is less than m (C1 holds).

(C2 holds) To show that C2 of Lemma 5 holds, we have to show that Γ L is special on m ′ processors where m ′ = (m -|Γ H |). Let UL be the total utilization of all the tasks in Γ L . Also let u maxL and u minL be the maximum utilization and minimum utilization of any task in set Γ L , respectively. Lemma 1 was originally derived in [1] for implicitdeadline task systems. However, it is easy to see that Lemma 1 is also applicable to constrained-deadline task systems by (i) considering density rather than utilization, and (ii) performing the schedulability analysis of a lower priority task τ j within a scheduling window of length D j rather than T j . Similarly, by considering density rather than utilization of the tasks, all Lemmas and Theorems, including the definition of "Special" task system, presented in this section are also applicable to constrained-deadline sporadic tasks. Consequently, if the total density of a constrained-deadline sporadic task set is not greater than m • min{1/2, B(m)}, then all deadlines are met using global FP scheduling where the priorities of the tasks are assigned based on HPA policy using the threshold density B(m).

div.head: V. TEST FOR CONSTRAINED-DEADLINE TASK SYSTEMS
div.p: In this section, we consider constrained-deadline sporadic task systems and propose an improved fixed-priority assignment policy for two state-of-the-art iterative schedulability tests: the RTA-LC test proposed by Guan et al. [15] and the DA-LC test proposed by Davis et al. [12].

The RTA-LC test is an improvement of the response-time analysis proposed by Bertogna et al. [7] for computing an upper bound on the response-time for each lower-priority task using the response time of the higher-priority tasks. The DA-LC test is an improvement of the schedulability test proposed by Bertogna et al. [9]. When testing the schedulability of a lower-priority task, both RTA-LC and DA-LC consider (m-1) higher-priority tasks to have carryin work within the scheduling window of the lower-priority task (based on Baruah's ideas in [6]). As shown in [12], the RTA-LC test dominates the DA-LC test for any given fixed-priority ordering of the tasks.

With respect to the applicability of Audsley's OPA algorithm [4], Davis et al. [11], [12] categorize a global FP schedulability test as being either OPA-compatible or OPA-incompatible. An OPA-compatible test implies that Audsley's OPA algorithm can be applied to find the optimal priority assignment using that test. Davis et al. [12] proved that Audsley's OPA algorithm is applicable to the DA-LC test (OPA-compatible) but not applicable to the RTA-LC test (OPA-incompatible). It is also empirically shown in [12] that DA-LC combined with the OPA algorithm outperforms any RTA-LC test that uses some heuristic priority assignment (e.g., deadline-monotonic).

An overview of Audsley's OPA algorithm is given in Figure 2. Unlike the representation in [11], [12], we make the parameters (task set A, number of processors m and the OPA-compatible test S) of the OPA algorithm explicit.
Algorithm OPA(Taskset A, number of processors m, Test S) 1. for each priority level k, lowest first 2.
for each unassigned task τ ∈ A 3.
If τ is schedulable on m processors at priority k 4.

return "unschedulable" 9. return "schedulable" Figure 2. Optimal priority-assignment algorithm. It is the same as the algorithm presented in [11], [12] except that the parameters -task set A, number of processors m and schedulability test S -are made explicit.

The algorithm in Figure 2 reveals an interesting fact, namely that the priority-assignment policy that uses the combination of the OPA algorithm and an OPA-compatible schedulability test only claims to be optimal under the assumption that this combination is applied to the entire task set and to all processors (Theorem 3 in [12]). An intuitive question to ask is then whether it would be possible to obtain a more effective priority assignment for the OPA-compatible test if the combination of the OPA algorithm and the OPAcompatible test was applied to find the priorities of a subset of the entire task set to be scheduled on a lower number of processors while the remaining tasks are assigned fixed priorities using some other mechanism (e.g., the highest fixed priority using the HPA policy). By carefully studying the equations of the DA-LC test (an OPA-compatible test), we find that there is indeed room for improvement. In this section, we employ the HPA policy to the combination of the OPA algorithm and DA-LC test in order to find a better priority assignment policy using the DA-LC test. Moreover, we also find that the HPA policy can also be applied to the OPA-incompatible RTA-LC test.

We now present the DA-LC [12] and RTA-LC [15] tests for constrained-deadline task systems as a means for understanding our improved HPA-based priority-assignment policy. The following equations, (Eq. ( 23) -( 31)), are presented in a different form than used in [15], [12] in order to show the similarities and differences between RTA-LC and DA-LC. In the remainder of this section, we call the higher priority task τ i a "carry-in task" (CI) if it is considered to have carry-in work; otherwise, τ i is called a "non-carry-in task" (NC).

Note that R i is an upper bound on the response time of the higher priority task τ i and is calculated before R k is calculated. The improved priority-assignment policy we propose for the DA-LC test is based on a crucial observation of Eq (25). When computing the interference I k (D k ) in Eq. ( 25), for testing the schedulability of τ k on m processors using the DA-LC test, the higher priority tasks are in hp(k) and the number of CI tasks considered is (m -1). Our observation is that, if we remove one task, say τ h , from hp(k) and also reduce the number of processors from m to (m -1), and apply the DA-LC test on this smaller task set and reduced number of processors, then the interference I k (D k ) depends on the the higher priority tasks in set (hp(k) -{τ h }) and on (m -2) CI tasks. To understand the importance of this observation, consider the following example. Example 1: Consider four tasks in Γ={τ 1 , . . . τ 4 } to be scheduled on m = 3 processors using global FP scheduling. The parameters (C i , D i , T i ) of the four tasks are as follows: (23, 33, 33), (106, 210, 214), (58, 216, 217), and (46, 60, 64). The call OPA(Γ, 3, DA-LC) returns "unschedulable" because no task in Γ can be assigned the lowest priority. This is because, when the schedulability of each τ k ∈ Γ is checked as the lowest priority task (line 3-5 of OPA algorithm in Figure 2), the calculation of I k (D k ) using Eq. ( 25) considers (m -1) = 2 tasks in hp(k) as CI tasks and the remaining task in hp(k) as NC task. The value of I k (D k ) for all the four tasks was large (pessimistic) enough to violate Eq. ( 23) and no task is decided to be assigned the lowest priority and the OPA algorithm returns "unschedulable". Now consider hybrid-priority assignment in which the highest density task τ 4 is given the highest fixed priority. We call OPA({τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 }, 2, DA-LC) by removing τ 4 from Γ and reducing the number of processors from m = 3 to m = 2. In this case, the OPA algorithm returns "schedulable". This is because, when OPA({τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 }, 2, DA-LC) is called, the calculation of I 3 (D 3 ) in Eq. (25) considers only (m -1) = 1 task in hp(3) as CI task and one task in hp(k) as NC task. In this case, I 3 (D 3 ) was small enough to satisfy Eq. (23) and τ 3 is assigned the lowest priority. The other two tasks, τ 1 and τ 2 , are trivially assigned the highest fixed priority since there are two processors. Hence, OPA({τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 }, 2, DA-LC) returns "schedulable". Since τ 4 is assigned the highest fixed priority and OPA({τ 1 , τ 2 τ 3 }, 2, DA-LC) returns "schedulable", this instance of HPA guarantees that Γ is schedulable on m = 3 processors (from Observation 1 following Lemma 5).

The important conclusion from this example is that, if the schedulability of Γ cannot be decided on m processors by applying the combination of the OPA algorithm and the DA-LC test to the entire task set Γ and to m processors, it does not necessarily mean that there is no feasible priority assignment for Γ based on the DA-LC test. The lesson learned is that the upper bound on interference I k (L), calculated based on DA-LC using Eq. ( 25), may be lowered by not including all the tasks and all the processors in the corresponding schedulability test. The HPA policy can exploit this because it provides "separation of concerns" in the sense that (i) OPA combined with DA-LC can be applied (due to the predictability of global FP scheduling) only to the (nk) lowest-density tasks to be scheduled on (mk) processors and (ii) the remaining k highest-density tasks are assigned (without any concern) the highest fixed priority for some k, 0 ≤ k < m.

This combination of the HPA policy together with algorithm OPA and DA-LC is called the hybrid-priority DA-LC U/m for utilization level U and the y-axis represents the acceptance ratio. It is evident from Figure 5 that the effectiveness of both HP-DA-LC and DA-LC are the same (100% acceptance ratio) at low utilization levels (e.g., when utilization is below 0.5m). However, the difference between the acceptance ratios of the HP-DA-LC and DA-LC tests become noticeable at higher utilization levels. We have found a similar trend for other experiments with parameters m = 2, 4, 8 and n = 2m, 6m, 8m. The reason for this trend is that there are relatively larger number of high-density tasks at higher utilization levels for a given task set cardinality. Some of these high-density tasks are assigned the highest fixed priority based on the HPA policy and receive their own processor while the other (low-density, lower-priority) tasks are checked for schedulability on a fewer number of processors using the HP-DA-LC test. As a result, the pessimism regarding the upper bound on interference due to the high-density, higher-priority tasks is lower for the HP-DA-LC test than for the DA-LC test. Consequently, the HP-DA-LC test performs relatively better than the DA-LC test at high utilization levels. In order to measure the extent of the improvement of the HP-DA-LC test, we perform a second set of experiments.

Experiments to measure improvement: We conduct our second set of experiments to measure the improvement of the HP-DA-LC test over the state-of-the-art DA-LC test using a metric that we call exclusive-passed ratio. This metric is calculated as follows: we generate task sets such that all 100 task sets generated at each utilization level U pass the HP-DA-LC test. The exclusive-passed ratio at utilization level U is the percentage of these 100 task sets that do not pass the DA-LC test at that utilization level.

We conducted 4 experiments (m, n) where m ∈ {4, 8} and n ∈ {2m, 6m}. Since the improvement of the HP-DA-LC test exists only at high utilization level, we determine the exclusive-passed ratio only at the 20 higher utilization levels {0.5m, 0.525m, . . . 0.975m, m}. The outcome of these 4 experiments are presented in Figure 6, where the x-axis represents system utilization U/m and the y-axis represents the exclusive-passed ratio.

It is evident from Figure 6 that the exclusive-passed ratio increases as the utilization level increases and then Exclusive-passed ratios to measure improvement of HP-DA-LC over DA-LC. (Observe that there are some data points missing on the right-hand side of the curves. This is because generating 100 random task sets that all pass HP-DA-LC at a very high utilization level was not possible; and in such case the task-set generation algorithm was aborted.) decreases sharply at very high utilization levels. In general, the exclusive-passed ratio in experiments with larger taskset cardinality (i.e., n = 6m) is higher than that of task sets with smaller cardinality (i.e., n = 2m). This is because at high utilization levels there is a relatively larger number of high-density tasks in a task set with small cardinality. And dedicating one processor for each of these high-density tasks using the HPA policy causes the low-density tasks to fail the HP-DA-LC test on a relatively lower (i.e., insufficient) number of processors. Consequently, the exclusive-passed ratio for larger cardinality task sets is relatively larger. However, the exclusive-passed ratio for low-cardinality task sets still offers good performance. For example, the exclusive passedratio for m = 8 and n = 2m peaks at 75% at utilization level 0.85m.

The conclusion from our experimental study is that, even though a relatively low number of randomly-generated task sets having large total utilization pass the HP-DA-LC test, the improvement of the HP-DA-LC test over the DA-LC test at high utilization level is significant.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we have derived an improved utilization bound that is higher than other existing utilization bounds for global FP scheduling of implicit-deadline sporadic task systems and also given guidelines of how to extend this result to constrained-deadline tasks. We have also improved the priority-assignment policies of the current state-of-the-art iterative schedulability tests RTA-LC and DA-LC for global FP scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic task systems. While the OPA algorithm is not applicable to the RTA-LC test, we find that our HPA policy is indeed applicable to the RTA-LC test. Our proposed HP-RTA-LC and HP-DA-LC tests dominate the state-ofthe-art iterative schedulability tests RTA-LC and DA-LC, respectively.

Using Observation 1 following Lemma 5, the entire task set Γ is global FP schedulable if the (nk) lowest-density tasks are feasible using the RTA-LC test on (mk) processors for some k < m. For a given priority assignment for Γ, it is not hard to see that the hybrid-priority RTA-LC (HP-RTA-LC) test dominates the RTA-LC test.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we present our experimental results to measure the effectiveness of our proposed HP-DA-LC test and its improvement over the DA-LC test. By "effectiveness" of the HP-DA-LC test we mean the percentage of randomly generated task sets that pass the HP-DA-LC test at different utilization levels. By "improvement" of the HP-DA-LC over the DA-LC test we mean the percentage of task sets that passed the HP-DA-LC test but did not pass the DA-LC test (remember that HP-DA-LC dominates DA-LC). Before the experimental results related to these measures are presented and analyzed, we present the task set generation algorithm for our experiments.
